FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Explain how to evaluate patients who report pain or dysfunction after total hip arthroplasty.
Review the differential diagnosis for patients with pain or dysfunction after total hip
arthroplasty.
Identify the patient history, physical examination findings, laboratory study findings, and
imaging study findings indicative of a failed total hip arthroplasty implant.

1/23

Total hip arthroplasty (THA) has become one of the most common and popular
procedures in orthopaedics, with an estimated 460,000 to 512,000 projected THA
procedures to be performed in the United States in 2020.1 Although most patients
report substantial improvements in pain and function after THA, a minority of patients
will report at least some degree of new or continued pain and dysfunction
postoperatively.2
Evaluation
Pain and dysfunction after THA may result from various causes. The common differential
diagnosis for a painful THA implant includes the following:
Infection
Instability
Aseptic loosening
Bearing wear/disease
Component malpositioning
Taper corrosion
Iliopsoas impingement
Extra-articular sources

Evaluation
Possible etiologies of THA implant pain are broad and may share similar signs and
symptoms. Surgeons must be systematic in their evaluation of patients with a painful
THA implant to determine the correct diagnosis and initiate appropriate management. A
thorough evaluation includes a review of the patient history, physical examination
findings, laboratory studies, and imaging studies. These investigations should be
continued, and potentially repeated, until a plausible reason for the patient’s symptoms
has been identified. Revision surgery should not be undertaken without an established
cause of dysfunction or pain.

Patient History
A complete history of a patient’s pain after THA may help identify the possible sources.
Inquiries should be made that focus on identifying the following:
When and how the symptoms appeared
For example, pain starting in the postoperative period that did not have any period of
improvement may be concerning for acute periprosthetic infection. Conversely, a
previously well-functioning hip with pain that occurs many years postoperatively may be
concerning for osteolysis or a late hematogenous infection.
Exact location of pain
Symptoms in the anterior hip/groin may suggest implant failure, whereas symptoms in the
lateral thigh may suggest an extra-articular problem, such as trochanteric bursitis or
iliotibial band syndrome.
Duration of symptoms
Symptoms that were present preoperatively and have continued unchanged may be
indicative of an extra-articular problem, such as radiculopathy or a low-grade infection.
Nature or characteristics of the pain
Burning pain or paresthesia is suggestive of a radicular or neurologic source. Audible
noises or squeaking may be a sign of ceramic-on-ceramic articulations.
Aggravating or alleviating factors
Pain that appears with movement and improves with rest may be concerning for a
mechanical problem; however, pain that is continuous may suggest an inflammatory
process, such as infection.
Start-up pain with the first few steps or immediate–weight-bearing pain on rising from a
seated position may be indicative of component loosening.
Responses to management
Severity of symptoms
Mild pain, particularly if present for only a short time, may be suggestive of a minor soft-
tissue strain, whereas incapacitating pain requiring a wheelchair or ambulation assistance
may be concerning for occult fracture or loosening.

Patient History
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
3/23

A review of the patient’s medical and social histories may provide valuable information
on his or her baseline risk for certain complications. Suspicion for infection should be
increased in patients who have a history of septic arthritis, prolonged wound drainage,
and persistent pain after arthroplasty. In addition, patients with morbid obesity, diabetes
mellitus, kidney disease, or autoimmune disorders or who smoke may have an increased
risk for infection. Patients with a history of neurologic disorders, such as Parkinson
disease; a history of lumbar fusion; or mixed connective tissue disorders may have an
increased risk for postoperative instability. Similarly, a history of neuropathy and spinal
disease may be the source of extra-articular causes of leg pain after THA. A review of the
patient’s surgical report and implant record also may be helpful. This information can aid
in the identification of recalled implants, sources of modularity, and bearing surfaces
used in THA, which may help suggest a complication that is known to be uniquely related
to a particular implant design or material. In addition, review of preoperative
radiographs may be useful to confirm degenerative changes in the hip.
Physical Examination
A comprehensive physical examination can provide invaluable information in evaluating a
patient with a painful THA implant. This requires a general inspection of the patient, gait
evaluation, neurologic examination, vascular examination, and thorough musculoskeletal
examination, including the following:
Visual inspection of the incision site and the surrounding skin
Palpation of adjacent bone and soft tissue
Evaluation of range of motion of the involved hip and the adjacent joints
Testing of extremity strength
Testing of the stability of the involved hip
Comparison of limb length of the involved extremity with that of the contralateral extremity
Assessment of gait, particularly gait velocity and presence of a limp
Laboratory Studies

Laboratory Studies
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Workup in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
4/23

Serum erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) level should be
routinely obtained in evaluating a painful THA implant. These laboratory studies are
used to screen for periprosthetic infection, which may present as nonspecific signs and
symptoms mirroring various other diagnoses. Additional laboratory studies are not
routinely necessary; however, ESR and CRP level are concerning or if clinical suspicion for
periprosthetic infection is high, then additional laboratory workup may be necessary.
Typically, this includes synovial fluid aspiration for culture and evaluation of synovial
white blood cell (WBC) count and polymorphonuclear leukocyte differential. If specific
concern for metallosis related to articular bearing wear or taper corrosion exists, then an
evaluation of serum cobalt and chromium levels also may be indicated.
Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
Every evaluation of a painful THA implant requires imaging studies. A complete set of
plain radiographs of the hip in question, including at least two orthogonal views, should
be obtained. Component size and position should be carefully reviewed on these
images, and the periprosthetic bone should be evaluated for signs of fracture, osteolysis,
or radiolucency. Comparing current radiographs of the THA implant with earlier
radiographs may help identify subtle changes in component positioning or the
periprosthetic bone. Additional imaging studies may be indicated, depending on the
level of suspicion for a diagnosis. Examples may include plain radiography of the knee or
spine, CT of the hip, MRI with metal-artifact reduction sequences (MARS) of the hip,
ultrasonography of the hip, and nuclear medicine studies.
Differential Diagnosis
Infection
Definition
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Workup in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
5/23

Superficial or deep development of bacterial, mycobacterial, or fungal contamination of the
joint (Resources 1 and 2).
Infection may be the result of direct inoculation or may be hematogenous.
Acute infection is defined as that developing within 6 weeks of the index procedure.
Chronic infection occurs if more than 6 weeks after the index procedure.
In defining infection based on the onset of symptoms, if pain and infection are diagnosed
within 3 to 4 weeks of symptoms, management may involve retention of the arthroplasty
components and exchange of the modular parts with irrigation and débridement
(débridement, antibiotic agents, and implant retention). If symptoms are ongoing for more
than 4 weeks, management typically involves explantation of the primary components,
extensive débridement, and insertion of a temporary antibiotic spacer.
Patient History
Patients with a prosthetic joint infection usually present with increased or persistent pain in
the affected joint. A painful total joint should be considered infected until proved otherwise.
Patients may report that their joint never felt quite right.
Other symptoms include difficulty bearing weight or decreased range of motion because of
pain or stiffness.
Patients also may have overlying cellulitis, warmth, or wound drainage.
Constitutional symptoms, such as fever, chills, or rigor, are reported if the infection is severe or
systemic.
Physical Examination
Antalgic gait
Peri-incisional erythema
Wound drainage
Sinus tracts (Figure 1)

Figure 1 Clinical photograph shows a total hip arthroplasty incision with an adjacent sinus
tract. A = anterior, I = inferior, P = posterior, S = superior. (Reproduced from Abdel MP, Hansen
AD: Management of the infected total hip arthroplasty, in Lieberman JR, ed: Advanced
Reconstruction: Hip, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp
327-334.)
Fluctuance
Pain with range of motion
In some patients, the physical examination may be normal.
Laboratory Studies
The diagnosis of infection is largely based on the 2018 guidelines developed by the
Musculoskeletal Infection Society. These criteria have been validated.3
Major criteria: two positive cultures of the same organism or a sinus tract with evidence of
communication to the prosthesis
If either of the major criteria are satisfied, then the joint is infected.
Minor criteria—A point value is assigned to each criterion. If the total point value is greater
than or equal to 6, then infection is diagnosed. If the total point value is 3 to 5, the joint may be
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Workup in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
7/23

infected and additional intraoperative criteria are required for definitive diagnosis. If the total
point value is less than 3, the joint is not infected.
2 points: elevated CRP (>1 mg/dL) or D-dimer (>860 ng/mL) level
1 point: elevated ESR (>30 mm/h)
Synovial markers
3 points: elevated synovial WBC count (>3,000 cells/mm3 for chronic infections, >10,000
cells/mm3 for acute infections) or ++ leukocyte esterase
3 points: positive alpha defensin level (signal-to-cutoff ratio >1)
2 points: elevated synovial polymorphonuclear leukocyte percentage (>90%)
1 point: elevated synovial CRP level (>6.9 mg/L)
If the previously mentioned minor criteria are inconclusive (ie, 3 to 5 total point value), the
following values are added to the preoperative point value.
3 points: positive purulence
3 points: positive histology
2 points: single positive culture
If the total point value is greater than or equal to 6, the joint is considered infected. Values of 4
or 5 are inconclusive. A value less than or equal to 3 is considered not infected.
Laboratory values should be used in combination with the overall clinical patient presentation.
Molecular testing, such as next-generation sequencing, has shown promising results.4
Imaging Studies
Radiography: first-line imaging modality for a painful THA implant to evaluate for gross signs of
loosening, malpositioning, or infection; radiographs should be compared serially to previous
radiographs to assess for any changes.
Signs of infection include bone resorption and periprosthetic lucencies.
Nuclear medicine studies
In general, involves labeling of leukocytes with the use of radioactive tracers to highlight
areas of infection
Bone scintigraphy
Technetium-99m scintigraphy or indium-111–labeled leukocyte scintigraphy allows
leukocyte radioactive–labeled diphosphonates to migrate to areas of bone mineral matrix
with high levels of activity and blood flow, as in infection. Although specific for joint
infection, this test is associated with poor sensitivity.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Workup in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
8/23

Most sensitive if performed 2 to 5 years after the index procedure because bony
remodeling after THA may lead to a false-positive result
Consists of three phases: the early phase (or perfusion phase); the blood pool or soft-tissue
phase, with static images of the region of interest; and the late phase, acquired
approximately 2 to 4 hours after injection
Infection may be suspected if blood pool and late images show increased uptake at the
prosthesis interfaces.
A normal scan is most suggestive that no loosening or infection is present; however, a
positive scan is associated with difficulty distinguishing among infection, aseptic
loosening, and postoperative changes.
Fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography enables visualization of inflammatory
cells during infection based on glucose uptake and increased cellular metabolism. This
imaging modality requires only one injection and is readily available. This imaging modality
also is highly sensitive.
Sulfur colloid: used as a supplement to scintigraphy by evaluating bone marrow activity to
increase the sensitivity of testing
Both WBCs and sulfur colloid accumulate in marrow regardless of location; however, WBCs
increase in infection and sulfur colloid does not.
Increased activity on the WBC images without corresponding activity on the marrow images
should be interpreted as positive for infection.5
Sulfur colloid that has been improperly prepared or that is more than 2 hours old may
degrade image quality and lead to incorrect results.6
Aseptic Loosening
Definition
Separation or loss of stable fixation between the implant and cement, cement and bone, or
implant and bone in the absence of infection.
Aseptic loosening is one of the most common indications for modern revision THA.7
This failure may be the result of inadequate initial fixation at the time of the index procedure,
excessive or pathologic mechanical forces on the implant over time, or periprosthetic
osteolysis related to chronic activation of macrophages by wear debris.
Patient History

9/23

Pain that increases with weight bearing
Start-up pain or pain at the initiation of activity that subsides with increased movement
Groin pain may be suggestive of acetabular component loosening, and thigh pain may be
suggestive of femoral component loosening.
Physical Examination
Often normal or unremarkable physical examination findings
May have minimal to no pain with hip range of motion if subtle loosening is present or pain
throughout hip range of motion if components are grossly loose
Pain predominantly with active range of motion or only at the extremes of motion also may
occur.
Laboratory Studies
ESR and CRP level should be obtained to screen for infection.
Imaging Studies
Current plain radiographs of the hip should be obtained and compared with previous
radiographs to evaluate for signs of loosening.
Component shift or migration
New or progressive radiolucent lines at the bone-cement, implant-cement, or bone-implant
interface
Particularly if lines develop or change more than 2 years postoperatively
Fracture of cement mantle or component
Cementless femoral stems with a bony distal pedestal
Cementless femoral stems without signs of bone ingrowth, such as endosteal spot welds or
calcar atrophy
If clinical suspicion for loosening is high and plain radiographs are unremarkable or
inconclusive, bone scintigraphy may be indicated; however, results should be interpreted
carefully.
Increased uptake around an implant may be suggestive of infection, loosening, or stress
fracture.
Increased uptake around an implant also may be observed in normal, well-functioning hips
as long as 2 years after routine THA.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Workup in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
10/23

Bone scans are not routinely obtained within the first 12 to 18 months postoperatively
because they may lead to false-positive results.
Bone scans are most useful if they are completely normal; then loosening usually can be
ruled out.
Instability
Definition
Subluxation or dislocation events after THA leading to pain and discomfort.
Instability after primary THA ranges from 0.3% to 10% and in the revision setting may be as
high as 28%.
Most dislocations occur within the first 3 months after the index procedure; however, a
dislocation can occur any time postoperatively.
Patient History
The patient may report an inciting event, such as a fall, a twisting event, bending at the waist
beyond 90°, or sitting in a low chair. Depending on the surgical approach, different positions
are more conducive to dislocation.
Anterior approach: more likely to dislocate in positions of hip extension and external rotation
Posterior approach: more likely to dislocate in positions of hip flexion and internal rotation
Patient risk factors
Female sex
Neuromuscular disease
Cognitive disorders
Previous hip surgery
Abductor weakness or insufficiency
Spinal fusion or stiffness
Alcoholism
Physical Examination
Patients may feel a sensation of instability during range of motion testing of the hip.
Evaluate abductor strength
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Workup in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
11/23

Laboratory Studies
Laboratory tests are not routinely necessary to establish the diagnosis; however, ESR and CRP
level should be obtained to ensure that an infection is not present.
Imaging Studies
Radiographs, including an AP pelvis view and AP and cross-table lateral views of the hip, to
evaluate for gross abnormalities or implant position changes compared with previous
radiographs
Radiographs also should be critically analyzed to determine the following:
Component position
Head size
Head-to-neck ratio
Offset
Leg-length discrepancy
A CT scan may be obtained to further evaluate component positioning.
Lumbar spine seated and standing radiographs or EOS imaging studies should be obtained to
evaluate pelvic mobility and the possibility of a stiff spine contributing to instability.
Patients with a stiff spine and excessive lumbar lordosis and anterior pelvic tilt (ie, stuck
standing) have an increased risk for posterior dislocation in the seated position because
flexion of the femur leads to impingement on the anterior acetabulum and a posteriorly
directed force leading to dislocation.
Patients with a stiff spine and flat back deformity with posterior pelvic tilt (ie, stuck sitting)
have an increased risk for anterior dislocation because of increased functional anteversion.
Bearing Wear or Disease
Before the introduction of highly cross-linked polyethylene in the late 1990s, conventional
polyethylene was used in THA.
Sterilization and processing of the materials involved gamma irradiation to induce cross-
linking; however, in the presence of oxygen, free radicals were not able to be quenched.
Therefore, the polyethylene became more brittle and less wear resistant.
Cyclic loading of the hip joint over time leads to the generation of debris and polyethylene
particles, which are then phagocytized by host macrophages, leading to peri-articular
osteolysis.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Workup in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
12/23

With the introduction of highly cross-linked polyethylene and improved sterilization processes,
the incidence of osteolysis has decreased drastically.
Hard-on-hard bearings (ie, ceramic-on-ceramic or metal-on-metal) result in lower wear rates
than polyethylene bearings but also are subject to problems, including squeaking or fracture
and metal ion disease.
Metal-on-metal THA implants were associated with frequent adverse local tissue reactions
(ALTRs) and are no longer available for clinical use.
Definitions
Volumetric wear—Wear directly proportional to the square of the radius of the femoral head.
Larger femoral heads are associated with higher rates of volumetric wear. This type of wear is
directly proportional to the number of particles generated.
Linear wear: measured by the distance the femoral head penetrates the polyethylene liner
Smaller heads are associated with higher rates of linear wear but lower rates of volumetric
wear.
Larger femoral heads are associated with higher rates of volumetric wear but lower rates of
linear wear.
Excessive wear is defined as more than 0.1 mm/year (osteolysis threshold).
Laboratory Studies
ESR and CRP level should always be obtained to ensure that infection is not present.
In patients with a metal-on-metal bearing, serum cobalt and chromium levels should be
obtained to evaluate and monitor for possible metal ion disease.
Imaging Studies
Radiographs will demonstrate eccentric polyethylene wear. This should be evaluated by
comparing the distance from the edge of the femoral head superiorly and inferiorly to the
edge of the acetabulum. The inferior distance typically is larger than the superior distance,
indicating asymmetric wear.
MARS MRI is useful to identify pseudotumors around the joint associated with ALTRs.
Component Malpositioning
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Workup in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
13/23

Incorrect or abnormal placement of acetabular or femoral components in THA may lead to
dislocation, pain, dysfunction, and decreased implant longevity.
Related complications include joint instability, accelerated wear, impaired muscle function,
soft-tissue irritation/impingement, bearing-related noise generation, limb-length discrepancy,
and aseptic loosening.
Definitions
Acetabular malpositioning includes incorrect or abnormal cup depth or mediolateral
positioning, cup height or superoinferior positioning, and cup angular positioning (inclination
and version).
Femoral malpositioning includes incorrect or abnormal neck length, neck angulation, stem
depth/penetration, stem angulation, and stem rotation.
Patient History
Patients may present with instability and chronic groin, thigh, or lateral hip pain.
Other complaints may include weakness, stiffness, hearing noises from the hip, leg-length
discrepancy, or a history of instability/dislocation events.
Patients with obesity and patients with a THA implant inserted via a minimally invasive
approach may be at greatest risk for malpositioning.8
Physical Examination
Patients may feel a sensation of instability during range of motion testing of the hip.
Audible noises, such as squeaking, may be generated during range of motion or gait testing.
Asymmetric clinical leg-length measurements may be observed.
Patients may demonstrate pain with resisted hip flexion or psoas stretch testing.
Patients may demonstrate tenderness to palpation and tightness at the greater trochanter or
along the iliotibial band.
Laboratory Studies
Laboratory studies are not routinely necessary to establish the diagnosis; however, ESR and
CRP level should be obtained to ensure that infection is not present.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Workup in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
14/23

Imaging Studies
Component malpositioning often will be readily apparent on plain radiographs of the hip. A
cross-table lateral radiograph is essential to determine the version of the acetabular and
femoral components.
Radiographic comparisons should be made to the native or contralateral hip, noting
differences in the location of the hip joint center, the amount of femoral offset, and leg
lengths.
If suspicion for malpositioning is high but standard plain radiographs are inconclusive, CT may
be helpful (Figure 2)
Figure 2 Axial CT scans of a hip with implant malpositioning. A, CT scan shows retroversion of
the acetabular implant. B, CT scan shows appropriate anteversion of the femoral stem by
overlaying the epicondylar axis of the knee onto the image. (Reproduced from Della Valle CJ,
Kayupov E, Rosenburg AG: Revision total hip arthroplasty: Indications and contraindications, in
Lieberman JR, ed: Advanced Reconstruction: Hip, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 389-395.)
Taper Corrosion
Definition
Damage and destruction of an implant taper because of mechanically assisted crevice
corrosion (Figure 3 ; Resource 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Workup in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
15/23

Figure 3 Intraoperative (A) and clinical (B) photographs of a total hip arthroplasty implant
show the deposition of chromium(III) phosphate because of fretting and crevice corrosion at
the femoral head-neck junction (A) and the neck-stem junction (B). (Reproduced from Taunton
MJ, Amanatullah DF: Taper corrosion after total hip arthroplasty: Evaluation and management,
in Lieberman JR, ed: Advanced Reconstruction: Hip, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 437-447.)
Implant modularity in modern THA may include modular femoral head-neck junctions and
modular femoral neck-body junctions. These modularity options offer many advantages. Most
notably, they may provide surgeons with convenient intraoperative and postoperative
flexibility, including the ability to easily adjust or revise femoral head size, femoral neck length,
and/or femoral neck angle during the index procedure or after implant failure.
However, these modular junctions can result in taper corrosion, potentially leading to
catastrophic failure from implant fracture or peri-articular tissue inflammation and destruction
from metal ion debris.
The resulting taper corrosion, also known as trunnionosis, reportedly accounts for 2% of
revision THA procedures.9
Patient History
The patient may report the onset of new pain or dysfunction several months or years after the
index procedure in a previously well-functioning hip.
Taper corrosion may occur with any material combination used at the modular junctions;
however, the greatest risk is observed if at least one of the junctional components is fabricated
from a cobalt-chromium alloy. For example, taper corrosion has been noted with the
combination of a cobalt-chromium femoral head and a titanium stem.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Workup in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
16/23

Risk of taper corrosion is increased if the patient has a large femoral head, long femoral
head/neck, varus stem, or high offset stem because these features can increase taper loads.9
Physical Examination
Soft-tissue destruction from a pseudotumor or ALTR may present as abduction weakness or a
Trendelenburg gait.
Laboratory Studies
If one of the junctional components is fabricated from a cobalt-chromium alloy, then serum
cobalt and chromium levels should be obtained to evaluate and monitor for possible metal ion
disease.
Elevated cobalt levels, particularly a substantial differential elevation of cobalt over
chromium is noted, may be suggestive of trunnion corrosion and ALTR.9 A cobalt level
greater than 1 ppb is a cause for concern.
ESR and CRP level should always be obtained to ensure that infection is not present.
If intra-articular aspiration is performed, a manual cell count should be requested because
metal debris may result in false elevation of automated cell counting processes.
Imaging Studies
Routine radiographs often will appear normal; however, osteolysis may be observed in
patients with advanced disease and bone-destroying ALTR.
A large femoral head, long femoral head/neck, varus stem, or high offset stem may be
identified on routine plain radiographs.
If clinical suspicion or laboratory studies are concerning, ultrasonography or MARS MRI may
help identify ALTR and the severity of any associated tissue destruction (Figure 4).

Figure 4 T1-weighted metal-artifact reduction sequence MRIs of a pelvis. A, Axial MRI shows
bilateral pseudotumors (arrows) involving the gluteus maximus muscle in the left hip and the
iliopsoas muscle in the right hip. B, Coronal MRI shows a pseudotumor (arrow) involving the
left hip capsule, with detachment of the abductor musculature. (Reproduced from Taunton MJ,

Increased capsular thickness, periprosthetic fluid, and complex synovitis are suggestive of
trunnionosis and tissue damage.9
Iliopsoas Impingement
Definition
Irritation and inflammation of the iliopsoas tendon after THA.
With a reported incidence of 4.4%, iliopsoas impingement is an underrecognized source of
pain and dysfunction after THA.10
Tendonitis of the iliopsoas is believed to be the result of mechanical irritation from the
following:
Acetabular component prominence at its anteroinferior margin
Retained cement near the iliopsoas tendon
Long acetabular screws penetrating the ilium
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Workup in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004023
18/23

Prominent femoral implant collars
Patient History
Patients classically describe overall well-functioning hips that generate intermittent pain in the
groin with certain activities.
Aggravating tasks include those that involve hip flexion, such as ascending or descending
stairs or getting in or out of a car.
Physical Examination
The patient may demonstrate pain with resisted hip flexion or psoas stretch testing.
Rarely, tenderness in the groin and a palpable painful snap during range of motion may be
detected.
Laboratory Studies
Laboratory studies are not routinely necessary to establish the diagnosis; however, ESR and
CRP level should always be obtained to ensure that infection is not present.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs, including an AP pelvis view and AP and cross-table lateral views of the hip,
may demonstrate the following:
Excessive retroversion or lateralization of the acetabular component
Relatively large/oversized acetabular component
Long acetabular fixation screws that penetrate the ilium
Retained cement near the iliopsoas tendon
Prominent femoral stem collar
Relatively large femoral head
Anterior acetabular prominence often can be best observed on true lateral radiographs.
Radiographic comparisons should be made to the native or contralateral hip, noting any
differences in femoral offset and leg length.
Increasing leg length and offset may excessively stretch the psoas tendon.
If clinical suspicion is high but standard plain radiographs are inconclusive, CT may aid in
evaluation of acetabular component size and positioning.
SEND FEEDBACK

An ultrasonography-guided iliopsoas tendon sheath injection may afford diagnostic and
therapeutic benefit.
Extrinsic Problems
Many sources of pain that can be felt in or around the hip after THA exist. These pain
generators are not always directly related to the implant or the joint itself.
Common extrinsic or extra-articular sources of hip pain include disorders related to the
lumbar spine, such as radiculopathy from spinal stenosis, and injuries or inflammatory
processes involving adjacent soft tissues, such as trochanteric bursitis.
Less common extrinsic sources include vascular disease, neuropathic pain, femoral or inguinal
hernias, metabolic disease, insufficiency fractures, tumors, metastatic disease, and
retroperitoneal abscesses.
Patient History
Patients who report pain after THA similar to preoperative pain should increase suspicion for a
persistent or recurrent extrinsic source.
Lumbar spine disease should be considered in patients with the following:
Known history of lumbar spine disease or previous lumbar spine surgery
Pain that is predominantly located in the buttock or the side of the hip
Pain that radiates into the thigh or down to the foot
Paresthesia-like symptoms or pain associated with numbness, tingling, or burning sensations
Greater trochanteric bursitis should be considered in patients with pain that is predominantly
located in the buttock or the side of the hip or pain when lying on the affected side.
Vascular claudication should be considered in patients with a known history of vascular
disease or pain that resolves with rest.
Neuropathic pain should be considered in patients with diabetes mellitus or pain associated
with paresthesia-like symptoms.
Night pain or pain associated with night sweats or weight loss is concerning for tumor-related
etiologies.
Physical Examination
Pain with passive straight leg raise is suggestive of lumbar spine disease.
Tenderness to palpation of the lateral hip is suggestive of trochanteric bursitis. SEND FEEDBACK

Palpable swelling or masses around the hip may suggest a hernia or tumor.
Abnormal or diminished peripheral pulses may suggest vascular claudication.
Laboratory Studies
Laboratory studies are not routinely necessary to establish the diagnosis; however, ESR and
CRP level should always be obtained to ensure that infection is not present.
Imaging Studies
Pelvic radiographs obtained as part of routine hip evaluations often will include portions of the
lower lumbar spine, which may demonstrate lumbar spine disease if present (Resource 4).
Depending on the level of clinical suspicion, spine radiography, spine MRIs, pelvic MRIs, MARS
MRIs of the hip, vascular studies, or other imaging studies may be indicated.
